summary.text: A space probe is an uncrewed robotic spacecraft built to explore outer space and send scientific data back to Earth.
Unlike artificial satellites, which usually stay in orbit around Earth, probes are sent beyond Earth orbit toward other bodies or into deep space.
Probes are grouped by mission profile: flybys, orbiters, landers, rovers and atmospheric probes.

items.prompt: A probe passes close to a planet, then carries on without ever circling it. Which type is it?
items.explain: A flyby probe passes near a body without entering orbit; an orbiter is the type that circles its target.

items.prompt: Scientists want to keep studying one planet for a long stretch, not take a quick look. Which probe type fits?
items.explain: An orbiter stays around its target for long-term observation, while a flyby probe only passes near.

items.prompt: A team wants a craft that can drive across the ground after arriving on a moon. Which type does that?
items.explain: A lander reaches the surface, but a rover is the type that can move across it.

items.prompt: A craft drops down through a planet's gas envelope to learn what it is made of and what the weather is like. Which type is it?
items.explain: Atmospheric probes descend through an atmosphere to study its composition and weather conditions.

paragraphs.heading: What a space probe is
paragraphs.text: A space probe is a robotic spacecraft with no crew aboard, built to explore space and send scientific data back to Earth. Probes have been sent to the Moon, to planets and their moons, to asteroids and comets, to the Sun, and into interstellar space. They differ from artificial satellites, which mostly stay in orbit around Earth. A probe leaves Earth orbit and heads for another body or out into deep space.

paragraphs.heading: The first probes
paragraphs.text: The first probes were built in the late 1950s, in the early years of the Space Age. The Soviet Luna probes and the American Pioneer program were among the earliest. Those first missions were aimed at the Moon. Later ones reached farther: Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn and other worlds of the Solar System.

paragraphs.heading: Kinds of probes
paragraphs.text: Probes are sorted by what they do when they get where they are going. A flyby probe passes close to a world without going into orbit. An orbiter settles into orbit around its target so it can watch it for a long time. A lander touches down on the surface of a planet or moon, and a rover can drive across that surface. An atmospheric probe drops down through an atmosphere to measure what it is made of and what its weather is like.

paragraphs.heading: Landmark discoveries
paragraphs.text: Many probes have made important discoveries. Mariner 2 passed Venus in 1962, the first spacecraft to fly by another planet successfully. The Cassini–Huygens mission studied Saturn and its moons. Its Huygens lander came down on Titan in 2005, the first probe ever to land there.

paragraphs.heading: Out past the planets
paragraphs.text: The Voyager probes explored the outer planets and then kept going until they reached interstellar space. Voyager 1 crossed into it in 2012. No object made by people had been there before.

paragraphs.heading: Probes today
paragraphs.text: Modern probes keep reaching ever more distant parts of the Solar System. Recent missions aim for closer looks than any before them. Parker Solar Probe was designed to study the Sun, and Lucy was designed to study primitive asteroids.
